analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to pay cash compensation to passengers for airline-caused flight delays and cancellations.
analysis.headline: The bill to require airline delay compensation has been referred to an aviation subcommittee with five Democratic supporters and no vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directs the Transportation Department to write rules requiring airlines to pay passengers cash compensation when a flight is delayed or canceled for reasons within the airline's control. Passengers arriving 3 to 9 hours late would get up to $300; those arriving 9 or more hours late would get up to $775; anyone who misses a connection would get rebooked on the next available flight at no extra cost. These compensation rules would be in addition to the cash refunds passengers are already owed for canceled or significantly changed flights.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers whose flights are delayed or canceled for reasons the airline controls — staffing, maintenance, scheduling, and other airline decisions rather than weather or security. A traveler stuck for four hours could receive up to $300; one stuck overnight could receive up to $775, plus free rebooking for missed connections. Millions of Americans fly each year, and under current federal rules airlines owe refunds in some cases but no standard cash payment for long delays.

how_it_helps.text: Requires airlines to pay passengers up to $300 when an airline-controlled delay or cancellation makes them arrive 3 to 9 hours late, and up to $775 when they arrive 9 or more hours late [S2].
Requires airlines to rebook passengers who miss a connecting flight because of an airline-controlled delay or cancellation on the next available flight at no additional cost [S2].
Applies to both domestic and international flights, and covers delays or cancellations within the airline's control — not weather or other outside events [S2].
Makes clear these new payments are separate from and in addition to the refund rights passengers already have under federal law for canceled or significantly changed flights [S2].
Gives the Transportation Secretary one year after enactment to issue the regulations, so the payment rules would be set in detail by the department rather than by Congress [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The airlines pay: compensation checks, free rebooking, and the cost of operating flights that avoid triggering delays in the first place. Airlines argue these costs get passed into ticket prices, so frequent flyers and price-sensitive travelers could pay somewhat higher fares. Airlines currently face no federal requirement to pay cash compensation for delays.

drawbacks.text: The bill sets maximums ('not more than $300' and 'not more than $775') rather than fixed amounts, leaving it to the Transportation Secretary's regulations to decide what passengers actually receive — a later rulemaking could set payments well below the caps [S2].

Compensation applies only to delays 'within the control of the air carrier,' so weather, air traffic control problems, and other outside disruptions would pay nothing — the situations travelers most often blame airlines for would partly go uncompensated [S2].

Airlines would face new direct costs for payments and rebooking, which the industry commonly argues are recovered through higher ticket prices for all passengers, including those whose trips are never disrupted.

Determining whether a delay was 'within the airline's control' will require case-by-case judgments and dispute handling, which could create friction between passengers and airlines over individual claims.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For travelers, the benefit is direct and concrete: cash in hand when an airline's own decisions strand them for hours, and a free rebooking when they miss a connection. The main costs fall on airlines, and some may show up in fares; the caps also leave room for the actual payment amounts to be set lower than the headline numbers. On balance the bill transfers money and certainty from airlines to disrupted passengers, with the main design caveat that its guarantees depend heavily on how the Transportation Department writes the rules.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in mid-December 2025, referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, and in early February 2026 sent to its Aviation subcommittee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Emilia Strong Sykes introduced the Airline Passenger Compensation Act of 2025 in the House on December 17, 2025, joined by four Democratic cosponsors [S1].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, the committee that handles aviation legislation [S1].
On February 2, 2026, the bill was referred to the committee's Subcommittee on Aviation, a step short of a full committee markup or a floor vote [S1].
No further action appears in the bill's history, and Congress remains in session [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S. airlines are better off for now: with no committee hearing or vote scheduled, the current rule that airlines owe refunds but no standard cash compensation for long airline-caused delays remains in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Airlines, whose delay costs stay off the books

for.name: Rep. Emilia Strong Sykes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 17, 2025, requiring airline compensation for controllable delays and cancellations.

for.name: Reps. Rick Larsen, Greg Stanton, André Carson, and Julie Johnson
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, its only recorded support in Congress.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee / Aviation Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Took no action beyond the February 2, 2026 referral to the Aviation subcommittee — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record.

against.name: U.S. airline industry
against.what_they_did: Airline industry groups have historically opposed government-mandated cash compensation for flight delays, arguing delays are often outside airline control and mandates raise costs.

sides.party_line_note: All five recorded supporters — the sponsor and four cosponsors — are House Democrats, and no Republican support appears in the record.

industries.note: Airlines would owe cash payments of up to $300-$775 per affected passenger for delays and cancellations within their control, plus free rebooking for missed connections — costs they currently do not bear under federal rules. The industry's interest in avoiding this mandate runs against the passengers the bill compensates.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Aviation subcommittee with five Democratic cosponsors, no Republican support on record, and no hearing or markup scheduled. Transportation bills of this kind typically need committee action and bipartisan backing to reach the floor; with roughly a year left in this Congress, the most likely path is that it stays in subcommittee and expires without a vote unless supporters build broader coalition or attach the idea to a larger aviation reauthorization bill.
